For the September one it is the Moon: closeness is when you are understood without words, sensed, guessed, and a little mystery remains in the relationship. For the February one it is the Hermit: closeness is when it is calm next to someone, nobody demands immediate answers and silence is respected. Added together (18 + 9 = 27 → 9) these desires give the couple’s common language — the Hermit: together you would rather stay silent than start guessing out loud.

These desires are compatible but speak different languages. A typical scene. The September one has had a hard day. At home there is a silence with an invitation hidden in it: sense it and come over. The February one senses it — and that is exactly why they don’t come over: another person’s silence should be respected, since at such a moment they themselves would want to be left alone. The September one concludes: “they don’t care.” The February one: “I gave them space and got hurt feelings in return.” Both acted out of love, and both were left alone. This scene is the main one for your couple, and in other chapters we only refer to it.

The way out is to agree on translating from one language to the other. The September one should say at least one sentence: “I feel bad, sit with me” or “I feel bad, give me an hour, then come.” The February one should ask, even if they think they understand: “do you want to be alone or with me?” Guessing doesn’t go away; it just gets checked.

blocks.h3: Intimacy

blocks: Lisovskaya assigns physical intimacy to the couple’s material point, and you have Justice there. In intimacy it means mutuality: it must be good for both, and this can be talked about as calmly and directly as the budget. According to the book, a couple with Justice in its image is restrained in public but has love and passion, and the Sun in what fills you directly includes passion in what nourishes the union.

The difficulty here is a familiar one for you: desires are guessed rather than named. If one wants more tenderness, a different rhythm, more time without hurry, it is better to say it in words than to wait to be sensed. Your intimacy rests on three things: honesty — saying what you like and what you don’t; light — not only late in the evening when both are tired; and the novelty the Sun loves so much.

blocks.h3: Freedom by agreement

blocks: You both have the Fool as your dual; what this means for the compatibility of your characters is in the chapter on what each brings to the couple. In Lisovskaya’s plus the Fool means trust, and therefore a lot of freedom, supporting each other’s hobbies, friendship. In the minus — an uncertain status, the relationship as a game, no boundaries and no responsibility.

In the couple your two Fools add up to Justice. Your freedom rests on an agreement: each is free in what was agreed, and calm because they know the rules. An evening with friends without reporting, a trip by one of you, a hobby that takes time — all of this suits you if it is agreed in advance. To Justice, freedom that wasn’t agreed looks like a breach, and an overly detailed agreement smothers the Fool. Look for the middle: few rules, but clear ones.

blocks.h3: A separate word on jealousy

blocks: Among the Moon’s tasks the book names jealousy and hurt from made-up stories. Your couple has a clear mechanism for this: both need freedom, and the atmosphere is the Moon. One spent the evening with friends, came back happy and said little — it seems to them there is nothing to tell. The other fills in the picture: who they were with, why they are so cheerful, why they didn’t invite them. Nothing happened, but the other already has a version ready in their head, and it is not the kindest one.

Jealousy in your couple is rarely about a real threat and almost always about things left unsaid. So it is cured by the opposite of leaving things unsaid — by telling. The one who was free shares at least a couple of details: where they were, what was funny, whom they met. The one who is jealous talks about the feeling rather than accusing: “I felt uneasy, tell me how it went.” Such a story costs the Fool nothing, and for the Moon it replaces anxious fantasies with a living picture.

blocks.h3: When one of you is going through a hard time

blocks: Losing a job, a parent’s illness, the failure of an important project, simply a hard year — every couple has such periods, and your matrix shows well where the danger lies in them. The Hermit tells the one who is struggling to withdraw and cope alone. The Moon tells the other the worst versions, and the Hermit tells them not to intrude. Both one’s and the other’s Justice adds the thought “I have no right to burden the other.” In the end two people go through one trouble in different rooms.
What helps you in exactly such periods:

ul: **The one who is struggling names what they need:** “just be near”, “help with the chores”, “take my mind off it”, “give me a week, then we’ll talk”. Guessing during a hard period is especially difficult for both of you.
**The other offers something concrete, not general.** Not “if anything, I’m here”, but “today I’ll pick up the groceries myself and make dinner.”
**Agree on a time limit for silence.** The Hermit may withdraw, but with a clear return: “until the weekend”, “until the test results come.”

**Recount contributions for the time of trouble.** Your Justice loves equality, but in a hard year it is temporarily different: one carries more, and that is normal. Say it out loud so you don’t keep score later.

blocks: The book directly names one of the Hermit’s tasks: in difficulties not to hide in one’s shell but to help. For your couple a hard period is when this task gets solved fastest: having once gone through trouble together rather than apart, you remember for a long time that it can be done.

blocks.h3: How to talk about the future

blocks: Talks about the future are hard for your couple, and the reason is clear. The Moon in the atmosphere loves to dream but doesn’t like certainty. The Hermit in the common language wants to think everything through first. Justice in what joins you wants what is said to become a promise. As a result, dreaming out loud is a bit scary: what if the other takes a dream as a plan, and a plan as an obligation.

It helps to separate these talks. An evening of dreams — when anything can be said, without criticism and without obligations: “what if we lived by the sea”, “what if I quit my job and studied.” Nobody says “that’s unrealistic” or starts counting costs. A week later — an evening of decisions: out of everything that was said, you choose one thing and decide what to do with it this year. The Moon gets freedom, the Hermit gets time, Justice gets a result.

blocks.h3: What you strive for together

blocks: If you gather the relationship line into one goal, it comes out roughly like this: a home where each feels calm and can be themselves; a life in which it is clear who is responsible for what; and a shared movement into depth — towards your own work, your own knowledge, your own place. It is a quiet goal, and from the outside it may seem modest. But for a couple with the Hermit in its common language and values, depth is the main landmark, and there is no need to be ashamed of it in front of those who measure life by speed.
actions: Introduce the raw-thought rule: say any important wish out loud before the decision has ripened, and immediately set the day you will come back to the talk.
Agree on two phrases for a bad day — “sit with me” and “give me an hour” — and let each say which one is needed right now.
Together, make a short list of freedoms: what each can do without checking with the other, and what needs a warning at least a day ahead.
If the question of your relationship’s status is open, set aside a calm, separate talk for it.

chapters.h2: The couple as parents: fair order and a road of one’s own
chapters.conclusion: As parents you are a tandem that divides duties fairly and keeps the same rules for everyone. You teach younger ones to set a goal and walk towards it themselves. If there are no children, the same energies work in caring for each other and for the parents of both families.

cards.label: Parents in tandem
cards.caption: The inner circle to the left of the centre: how the couple supports each other as parents and how a child sees them. Justice.

cards.label: Attitude to the child
cards.caption: The small point between the large and the inner circle on the left: what the couple teaches younger ones. The Chariot: a goal and movement.

blocks: We don’t know whether you have children, and we won’t guess. The chapter is written for two cases: if there are or will be children — and if not. For a couple without children, Lisovskaya advises looking above all at the tandem point: how the partners support each other in caring.

blocks.h3: If there are or will be children

blocks: How a couple looks as parents is read from the inner circle to the left of the centre. You have Justice there, and it is made of your personal parents’ points: the September one’s Star and the February one’s Hermit, 17 + 9 = 26 → 8.

The Star in the September one’s parents’ point is inspiration and faith in the younger one, the ability to see their talent before they do. The February one’s Hermit is patience, the ability to give time to think and to explain why a rule is the way it is. How it can look: one tells the child “you can do it, I’ve seen how you draw”, the other sits down beside them and calmly works through what didn’t work and why. The tandem’s Justice is born not from strictness but from two adults telling the younger one the same thing — each in their own voice. If the voices start contradicting each other, the child will be the first to notice.

The attitude to the child — the small point on the left ray — is the Chariot for you. It is also made of your personal points, this time the children’s points: the September one’s Fool and the February one’s Empress, 22 + 3 = 25 → 7.

The September one’s Fool brings freedom, play, lightness and readiness to start over after a failure into upbringing. The February one’s Empress brings care, warmth and joy in how the younger one grows. One brings adventure, the other a nest, and together they give the Chariot: the younger one has a reliable home and a road they choose themselves. In Lisovskaya’s plus the Chariot means movement and clear roles, in the minus rivalry and tugging. There is no need to divide roles by gender: what matters is that you both have something to complement each other with.

How it can look in your couple. A child wants to quit music school in the middle of the year. Justice asks: what did we promise, what is fair to the teacher, to the child, to us? The Chariot asks: where do they want to move instead? A good answer comes if you discuss it first between the two of you, in private, and go to the child with a shared position. A bad one — if one says “you’ll finish until summer” and the other later quietly allows them to quit.

The risk of this combination is that order and goals can become cold. For the child of a couple with the Moon in the centre, it matters not only to know the rules but also to hear what you feel: “it hurts me that you lied to me” works more strongly than any prohibition. And another thing: in a couple where both love silence, a child may decide that the adults’ silence is about them. As with each other, it is worth telling them directly where your mood comes from.

formula.caption: **8 → 7 → 8.** The couple’s child–parent line: the Chariot between two Justices.

blocks: The couple’s child–parent line is Justice, the Chariot, Justice. The Chariot also stands in the middle of the material ray. The same energy — movement and the question of “who holds the reins” — meets you both in money and in parenting. In both places one thing helps: agreeing on roles in advance.

Lisovskaya also reads how a child sees you by the tandem point. Justice in it means that for the younger one you are a couple they can rely on: what was said will happen, rules don’t change with mood, and parents settle disputed questions between themselves rather than through the child. The price of this image is strictness: a child may feel there is no negotiating a concession with you. Leave them room for negotiation: the rule is shared, but an exception can be earned by asking for it honestly.

blocks.h3: If there are no children

blocks: The Justice tandem works without children too: in caring for each other and for those close to you. When one falls ill, the other takes over their share of the chores, and this is understood without long talks, because it is your habit to divide fairly. When one of the parents is going through a hard time, you decide together who will help and how.

A separate topic for a couple with Justice is the two families. Among the pluses of this energy the book names respect for the traditions of both families. Holidays taken in turn, equal help to parents without leaning to one side — for you this is no small thing. If you visit one family every weekend and the other once a year, sooner or later it will become a silent grievance. Most likely it won’t be said out loud — that is your way — which makes it all the more important to agree in advance.

The Chariot without children is the ability to support each other in your own movement: in study, career, sport, a move. You are good at helping each other set goals and reach them, as long as you don’t turn it into a race and don’t set the partner goals they didn’t ask for. Caring for younger ones in a broad sense belongs here too: nephews and nieces, godchildren, students, junior colleagues. A couple with the Chariot in this point is good at handing others the reins.

blocks.h3: How you support each other in caring

ul: **Inspire and explain.** In the parenting tandem one of you is the Star, the other the Hermit. When someone close is ill or going through a hard time, it is easier for the September one to support with hope and faith, and for the February one with patient explanation and time. Divide care by these roles, not equally by the hour.

**Adventure and a nest.** In your children’s points you have the Fool and the Empress: one knows how to entertain and pull someone out of routine, the other how to warm and feed. The person you are caring for needs both.

**Fatigue from caring.** The Hermit in the couple’s task pushes you to carry it in silence. In caring for loved ones this is especially dangerous: strength runs out unnoticed by the other, and they learn about it when it is too late to pick up the load.
**Recognition of care.** The Sun fills your couple with recognition. Care the other has noticed and named restores strength better than rest.

actions: Agree how you divide holidays and help between the two families, and write it down for the coming year.
If you are parents — before any disputed decision about a child, first discuss it between the two of you and go to the child with a shared position.
If there are no children — together, make an “if one falls ill” plan: who takes on what.

chapters.h2: The couple’s tasks: come out of your shell and don’t fill in each other’s picture
chapters.conclusion: Your couple’s task is not to hide each in yourself in difficulties and not to think for the other. Silence remains your strength if it is named, and sensitivity if guesses are checked. This task is easier to work through with small habits than with big talks.

cards.label: The couple’s main task
cards.caption: The large circle at the bottom. The Hermit in the minus: each on their own, problems pile up in silence.

cards.label: Middle of the tasks
cards.caption: The small point between the centre and the lower circle. The Moon: guesses, fears, half-tones.

blocks: Lisovskaya calls the couple’s line of tasks the couple’s karmic programme and immediately clarifies: some tasks are karmic, and some are simply life tasks. The main point is the large circle at the bottom; the other two unfold it. The line is read mainly through the minus: what doesn’t work for the couple and what it has to learn. Your programme is the Hermit, the Moon, the Hermit: the entrance to the task through the couple’s common language, the middle of the path, the main task.

formula.caption: **9 → 18 → 9.** The task begins and ends with the Hermit, with the Moon between them. The sum of all three, 36, again folds into a nine: the programme is closed on its main card.

blocks.h3: Entrance: a shared love of silence

blocks: A couple enters its task through what it wants together. You both want silence, a space of your own, unhurriedness. This is a real shared desire, and it joins you. But standing on the line of tasks, it also becomes resistance: it is convenient not to raise a difficult topic because “we both love silence anyway”. The better you are at being silent together, the easier it is to stay silent about what matters.

blocks.h3: Middle: the lunar stretch

blocks: In the middle of the task stands the Moon. The book gives this point no meaning of its own; it complements the main one. We read it as the path by which the couple goes from the shared desire to the task. In the river on the Moon card there is a small crayfish. Waite writes that the creature from the deep strives to climb out onto land but as a rule sinks back. A good image for your middle: the unspoken rises almost to words — and goes back, because the moment is wrong, the person is tired, “I’ll say it later”.

formula.caption: **18 = 18.** The Moon stands both in the couple’s centre and in the middle of its task. Your usual atmosphere is the very road by which you go towards the main task.

blocks: Among the Moon’s tasks the book names a habit of hiding feelings and seeing tenderness as weakness, hurt and jealousy from made-up stories, adjusting to the partner in a way that ends in irritation, quarrels out of nothing. For a quiet couple the first and third matter most. Each adjusts in silence, without saying they are uncomfortable — and then explodes over a trifle, and the other doesn’t understand where the explosion came from.

For example, one of you has agreed for years to spend holidays by the sea, though dreaming of the mountains. They don’t say so because the other loves the sea so much, and quarrelling over a holiday is silly. In the fifth year a forgotten sunscreen sets off a real quarrel: “I never wanted to come here in the first place!” The other is stunned — for five years they were sure both liked the seaside holidays. Neither lied. The truth simply never climbed out of the water onto the shore.

blocks.h3: How the task changes over the years

blocks: Among the Moon’s tasks there is one more, important for any long-standing couple: the image of the partner created at the start, which later collapses. At the beginning of a relationship the Moon helps you fall in love: much in the other you filled in yourself, and filled in beautifully. After several years of living together, a real person is beside you — with habits, tiredness, their own fears. For a couple with the Moon in the middle of its task this is the most delicate moment: what people are usually disappointed in at this point is their own drawing; the living person has nothing to do with it.

The same habit of asking helps to get through it. The more you know about what the other really thinks and feels, the less room is left for a drawing that can collapse. You live together, and everyday details — how each gets tired, what irritates, what brings joy — are your best material: each detail asked out loud replaces a guess with knowledge.

blocks.h3: The main task: don’t hide in your shell

blocks: The Hermit in the minus means each on their own, problems piling up in silence, work instead of family, one overshadowing the other, nitpicking and criticism. Lisovskaya formulates the tasks like this: in difficulties don’t hide in your shell, help; don’t stifle the partner’s interests; share and listen; more shared activity; build trust; sense when to support and when to leave alone.

Where the couple got this task and how to solve it can be seen in the personal matrices: the couple’s main task is made of your personal karmic tasks, 6 + 3 = 9. The September one’s personal karmic task is the Lovers: learning to feel openly, choose with the heart and talk about love. The February one’s is the Empress: learning care, warmth, the ability to enjoy life and accept joy from another. Both personal tasks are about openness and warmth. Added together they give the Hermit, the couple’s task of not hiding in a shell. So each, solving their personal task, also solves the shared one: when one learns to talk about feelings and the other to warm and accept warmth, the couple no longer needs to retreat to separate corners.

The last point is the core of your task. You both know how to leave someone alone. What you need to learn is something else: to understand when being left alone no longer helps, and to be the first to reach out to the other. Waite’s Hermit, by the way, is no runaway. Waite stresses that his figure has already reached the summit and holds up a light so that others can climb to it: “where I am, you also may be.” Solitude and returning to people are two halves of one card, and your couple needs both.

blocks.h3: The task and the values are one card

formula.caption: **9 = 9.** The Hermit stands both in the couple’s main task and in its spiritual purpose — its values.

blocks: This is an important coincidence, and it changes how you see the task. What is hardest for you — silence and withdrawing into yourself — is at the same time what you value most: depth, meaning, the right to your own path. So the task need not be solved by giving up silence. It is solved by filling silence with meaning: solitude from which you return with a thought and share it is valuable; solitude in which you hide is the task in the minus. The Hermit in the values also suggests a criterion: for you, good silence always ends in a conversation.

blocks.h3: What follows from what

blocks: Lisovskaya reads a couple’s programme by combinations: each conclusion states which combination of energies it follows from. Let’s try the same.

ul: **Talk about feelings before they become conclusions.** The Hermit thinks things through alone, the Moon thinks for the other; together you get a ready verdict that nobody discussed. (9 + 18)
**Tell solitude from hurt and say which one you are in right now.** Two silences side by side look the same from the outside. (9 + 9)
**Check a guess with a question.** The Moon in the middle makes the gloomiest versions seem plausible. (18)

**In difficulties, move towards each other, not into different rooms.** Fatigue, losses, a hard year are a test passed together or each alone; the second option cools the couple more than the difficulties themselves. (9 + 18 + 9)
**Don’t stifle each other’s interests.** The Hermit may find the partner’s hobby superficial, the Moon may be jealous of where the partner is happy without you. (9 + 18)
**Do more together.** A couple with this programme risks living in parallel, each in their own depth. A shared project, sport, a trip bring you back into one reality. (9 + 9)
**Trust without demanding proof.** The Moon asks for checks, the Hermit doesn’t like reporting. Trust grows from agreements that are kept. (18 + 9)

blocks.h3: How to work through the task so it doesn’t become a quarrel

blocks: The couple’s task turns into a quarrel when its solution is expected from the other: “let them speak first.” It can only be worked through together, and most simply with small regular actions.

ol: **Name your silence.** Accompany every withdrawal with the signal phrase you agreed on (in the couple’s key we suggested one). Five words instead of two days of guessing.
**Whoever noticed comes out first.** Not the one who is to blame and not the one who withdrew, but the one who first felt the chill. This rule removes the question “why me again”.
**A day for the unspoken.** If something hurt, you have a day to say so in at least one sentence. After that the trifle starts to grow.
**Check the version.** “It seemed to me that you… — is that so?” No conclusions until the answer.
**A phone-free evening once a week.** The Hermit needs depth, the Moon needs closeness. A long talk between the two of you gives both.

blocks: Lisovskaya has two pieces of advice for the Moon that your couple should keep together. The first: don’t take the partner’s withdrawal for a lack of love — that is how they recover. The second: talk about feelings and don’t think for others. The first without the second turns into a wall, the second without the first into an interrogation. Together they are the solution to your task.

This task is solved without heroics. It doesn’t need heavy talks until morning or re-educating each other. It needs five words at the right moment and a habit of asking instead of guessing. The Hermit doesn’t go anywhere: the silence stays yours, only now the other knows what is in it.
actions: Agree: whoever first noticed the chill is the first to come out of the silence.
Introduce the one-day rule: anything that hurt is named in at least one sentence within the day.
Once a year, for example on your anniversary, ask each other: “What did you agree to for my sake, though you wanted something else?”

chapters.h2: Where it breaks and how to fix it: four scenarios and a map of the rest
chapters.conclusion: Your quarrels are more often quiet than loud. They have a mechanism of their own in four places: plans that fall through, arguments about who is right, a dream against fear, and disputes about what to spend on. The other difficult spots are covered in the chapters on the areas of life — here is their map and the way-out phrases. A clear plan helps you make up.

cards.label: What can spoil things
cards.caption: The upper right corner. The Sun in the minus: comparisons, rivalry, control disguised as care.

cards.label: Main task
cards.caption: The large circle at the bottom. Together with the material point it shows what the couple may be doing wrong.

blocks: According to the book, a couple’s difficulties are looked for in several places. The upper right corner shows what quarrels arise over. The material point together with the main task shows what the couple does wrong in material and spiritual matters and what spoils the relationship. Repetitions show which themes sound loudest. Most of your difficult spots are already covered in the chapters on the areas of life, so here are only the scenarios with a mechanism of their own and a map of the rest.

formula.caption: **10 + 9 = 19.** The couple’s point of discord is added up from your personal points of influence — what each of you is easiest to hurt through.

blocks: Lisovskaya calls the upper right corner of a personal matrix the trigger: what a person is easiest to influence through. The September one has the Wheel of Fortune there, the February one the Hermit. If that is how it is for you, the September one is most easily thrown off balance by a change of circumstances: plans that fall through, sudden news, someone else’s decision that changes everything. The February one — by an intrusion into their silence or by disregard for what they have been thinking over for a long time. Together these two sensitive points give the Sun of discord.

blocks.h3: Scenario 1. Plans that fall through

blocks: **How it starts.** Something the September one counted on collapses: a trip is cancelled, an important meeting is moved, news arrives that changes everything. At that moment the February one is deep in their thoughts — thinking something over, finishing something, working on their own task. **How it develops.** The September one waits for sympathy, gets an absent-minded “mm-hm” and hears indifference in it. The February one, pulled out of concentration, gets irritated: the silence was broken, and what they were thinking over wasn’t taken seriously. Each was hurt exactly in their sensitive point, and both are sure the other hurt them first. **The way out.** Know your triggers and name them at once. The September one: “everything’s gone sideways, I need half an hour of your attention.” The February one: “I’m in the middle of a thought, give me ten minutes and I’m all yours.” Ten minutes is not a refusal, and it is easy to accept once it has been said.

Your material point and main task are Justice and the Hermit. Together they show what the couple may be doing wrong: counting in silence and withdrawing in silence. This scenario — a silent count of contributions — is covered in detail in the chapter on money, and withdrawing into yourself in difficulties in the chapter on the couple’s tasks.

blocks.h3: Scenario 2. An argument about who is right

blocks: **How it starts.** Where to spend the holiday, how to deal with a relative, whether to change jobs. Each has an honest position and arguments. **How it develops.** The argument stops being about the decision and becomes about who is right. Both bring ever new arguments and recall each other’s past mistakes. **The way out.** Waite’s Strength holds the lion with a chain of flowers: firmness without pressure. Agree on a simple rule: the goal of an argument is a shared decision. Whoever notices they are arguing to be right says: “Stop, I want to win, not to decide” — and the talk returns to the matter.

blocks.h3: Scenario 3. A dream against fear

blocks: **How it starts.** One lights up with a big change: a move, a new business, a big purchase. The Star at the entrance to money and the Tower in the point of abundance make such ideas frequent for you. **How it develops.** The other is afraid but says so not directly but through nitpicking at details. The first hears “you don’t believe in me” and is hurt. **The way out.** Split the dream into stages with checkpoints: what we do in the first three months, how much it costs, what happens if it doesn’t work out. The other’s fear is a valuable contribution: it makes the Tower manageable. So it is worth calling it fear rather than hiding it in nitpicking.

blocks.h3: Scenario 4. Bright against fast

blocks: **How it starts.** The September one wants to spend on something bright — give an expensive gift, arrange a trip, buy something that pleases the eye. At the same time the February one has lit up with something fast: paying for a course, starting a project, buying what the work needs right now. There isn’t money for everything at once. **How it develops.** Each considers the other’s spending optional and their own reasonable. Justice in the material point immediately gets out the scales: “last time it was already your way.” **The way out.** This is a clash of your two personal material points — the Sun and the Chariot — and neither is better than the other. The rules from the chapter on money help: each has their own pause and a line for joy, and disputed spending goes to the money evening, where the order of priority is decided, not who is right.

blocks.h3: Early signs by your points

blocks: A quiet couple can quarrel for a week without ever saying the word “quarrel”. Each of your main energies has its own early sign:

ul: **Justice:** a count has started in your head — who did how much, who sacrificed what;
**the Hermit:** conversations have shrunk to practical matters, evenings are spent in separate rooms;
**the Moon:** you have a ready version of what the other thinks, and you haven’t checked it;
**the Sun:** a barb appears in your voice when successes come up;
**Strength:** an argument about a matter has quietly become an argument about who is right.

blocks.h3: How to make up

blocks: Both of you have the Emperor as the point of reconciliation. You need a quarrel to end in clarity: what happened, who felt what, what we change. A good order of making up: first each says what they felt, and they are not interrupted. Then each says what their part was. Then one concrete agreement for the week. A hug comes at the end: for you it puts a full stop and doesn’t replace the talk.
actions: Each should know their trigger and name it at once: “everything’s gone sideways” or “I’m in the middle of a thought, give me ten minutes”.
Agree on a phrase for arguments about who is right: “stop, I want to win, not to decide”.
Move disputed spending to the money evening and decide the order of priority, not who is right.
Make up in three steps: what I felt, what my part was, what we change.

chapters.conclusion: Go through the couple’s main energies together and note where you are more often right now — in the plus or in the minus. Each answers alone, then compare: the differences will show what is worth talking about.
blocks: Read the questions aloud in turn. Don’t look for someone to blame: signs in the minus are what happens between the two of you, and nobody is to blame for them. If you recognise yourselves in both the plus and the minus of one energy, that is normal: that is how it works.

blocks.h3: How to do the self-check together

ol: **Each alone.** Take a sheet each and for every energy mark which statements are about you — from the plus and from the minus. Don’t confer and don’t peek.
**Comparison.** Put the sheets side by side. Where the answers match, everything is clear: this is your shared picture. Where they differ is the most interesting part.

**Differences — without arguing.** The one who marked a minus tells in what situation they see it. The other only listens and asks questions. There is no need to argue about who is right: each sees the couple from their own side, and both sides are real.
**One theme.** Choose one energy where there are the most minuses or the most noticeable difference, and start the plan from the next chapter with exactly that.

blocks: For your couple this exercise has a separate benefit. The Moon in the centre makes each sure they know what the other thinks. A self-check on paper is a way to test that certainty: it often turns out that the partner sees your couple more warmly than you thought, or notices what you considered unnoticeable.

selfcheck.label: Atmosphere and middle of the tasks
plus: We notice each other’s mood before it is mentioned.
You can tell the other a strange thought or fear without worrying it will be turned against you.

minus: We get hurt over what the other “should have sensed”.
We build theories about each other’s mood and rarely check them.
We agree on the matter but carry away hurt over the tone.

selfcheck.label: Main task and common language
plus: Each can be alone, and the other doesn’t take it as rejection.
We have long, deep conversations.
We don’t rush each other with decisions.
minus: We go through difficulties each in our own room.
Important decisions are put off for months because nobody is ready to speak first.
We live in parallel: side by side, but each in our own world.

selfcheck.label: Image, the material, what joins you
plus: We keep promises to each other, even small ones.
Money is clear to both: how much there is, where it goes, what is set aside.
Housework is divided, and both consider it fair.
minus: Each silently keeps count of who did how much.
We correct and judge each other in front of people.

selfcheck.label: What fills you and what spoils things
plus: We are proud of each other’s successes and say so out loud.
One’s growth pushes the other to grow too.

minus: We compare our successes.
One feels like a background next to the other.

plus: We know how to say an unpleasant truth gently.
Next to each other we become braver.

minus: An argument often becomes a fight about who is right.
One presses, the other gives way and keeps it inside.

selfcheck.label: Entrance to money
plus: We support each other’s projects and dreams.

plus: We dared big changes and came out of them stronger.

Changes happen to us rather than by our decision.
We see money differently and don’t discuss why.

selfcheck.label: Attitude to the child and movement
plus: We support each other in our own goals.
Each has their own development outside the couple.
Our roles in shared tasks are clear.
minus: We set each other goals nobody asked for.
Who holds the reins is an eternal argument for us.
Goals have crowded out joy.

blocks: If one row has more minuses, start the plan from the next chapter with exactly that row. If you and your partner answered differently, that is the topic of your next talk: one sees what the other doesn’t, and that is not a mistake by either of you. In three months, do the self-check again and compare.

chapters.h2: A plan for two: where to start
chapters.conclusion: Start with the loop of silence and guesses: agree on a signal for withdrawing and turn guesses into questions. Then a sunny day once a month for the couple and money order according to your resources. In a month, have one big talk about the future.

cards.label: Where to start
cards.caption: The couple’s main task and common language. The first step is to name your silence out loud.

cards.label: What to recharge with
cards.caption: The upper left corner: what fills the union. The second step is a sunny day once a month.

blocks.h3: Where to start and why

blocks: It is worth starting with the couple’s main mechanism — the loop of the Hermit and the Moon. It affects everything else: quarrels about money, comparisons, disputes about relatives flare up more strongly for you when unspoken things pile up between you. Break the loop and the other chapters will become easier. As the second step, bring the Sun back to the couple: silence restores you separately, while light charges the couple. As the third, money order distributed according to your resources: accounts, a plan for a big step, each with their own pause. It comes easily to you and quickly gives a sense of support.

blocks.h3: Right after reading

blocks: Each of you separately read “The main thing in a minute” and the chapter conclusions. Mark for yourself one point in which you definitely recognised your couple and one you doubt. Then swap marks — without arguing, just tell each other why. For a couple with the Moon in the centre this is already the first practice: you check in words what each thinks about your couple instead of guessing.

blocks.h3: The first step for tomorrow

blocks: Tomorrow evening, tell each other one sentence you haven’t said for a long time: “I’m proud of you for…” or “it hurt me when…”. One, no more. And agree on a signal for withdrawing — in your own words or the phrase suggested in the couple’s key.

blocks.h3: Habits for the month

ol: **Week 1. Name the silence.** Every withdrawal comes with a signal. Every anxious guess becomes a question. Before bed, briefly: what was good today and what hurt.
**Week 2. Light.** Have the first sunny day — a new place together. Celebrate out loud at least one success each.
**Week 3. Order.** Split money into a joint account, personal money and a change fund, decide who keeps the accounts, hold the first money evening. Put the division of housework somewhere visible.
**Week 4. Freedom and agreement.** Make a list of freedoms: what each does without checking, what with a warning. Sum up the month: what took hold and what didn’t.

blocks.h3: A talk worth having

blocks: At the end of the month, have one big talk — not at home, but where you both feel calm: on a long walk, on a trip, in a quiet place. The Hermit needs depth, Justice needs a result. Here are questions you can follow. Answer in turn and don’t argue with the other’s answer: first listen, then discuss.

ul: When in the past year did you feel I understood you without words? And when did I understand you wrongly?
Which of my silences frightens you, and which calms you?
Which success of each of us did we never celebrate?
What did you agree to for my sake, though you wanted something else?
What big change do we want in three to five years, and where do we start this year?
What is a fair contribution to our shared life for each of us?
What do we both need to feel free next to each other?

blocks: Afterwards, write down three agreements, no more. The Emperor in the point of reconciliation loves clarity for both of you, and long lists get in its way.

blocks.h3: The second and third months

ol: **Month 2. Money and a dream.** The second money evening, the first deposits into the change fund. If one of you has a talent people could pay for — the date of the first paid order. One postponed dream broken into stages: what we do in the next three months.
**Month 3. Family and care.** An agreement on holidays and help to the two families for the year. An “if one falls ill” plan. The second sunny day — organised by whoever didn’t organise the first.

blocks: For your couple a lapse is not dangerous in itself. What is dangerous is that the Hermit in the task prompts you to silently conclude: “it didn’t work out for us.” If a week went by without the plan, tell each other — “we dropped it, let’s get back to it” — and start from where you stopped.

blocks.h3: If you have very little time

blocks: If the whole plan feels too much, keep three things. The first is a signal for withdrawing. The second is one sunny day a month. The third is one concrete agreement at the end of every quarrel. These three habits cover the main things in your matrix: the loop of the Hermit and the Moon, the Sun that must shine on both, and the Emperor in each one’s point of reconciliation.

blocks.h3: In three months

blocks: Do the self-check again. If there are fewer minuses in the atmosphere and the task, the loop is breaking. If a change fund has appeared in your money and you know the first step, the Tower is working for you. If you remember at least two sunny days, the couple has fuel.

blocks.h3: Practices for the soul and for practical matters

blocks: The spiritual practices for your couple are those about attention and honesty. A silent walk together, after which each tells what they noticed. A short evening check-in: “what I felt about us today”. Thanking each other out loud for one concrete thing a day. The material ones are the budget, the change fund, the division of chores, the date of the first paid order for a talent that is still unpaid. For you one doesn’t hold without the other: the Moon needs clarity, Justice needs sensitivity.
actions: Tomorrow: one sentence long unsaid and an agreement on a signal for withdrawing.
In the next two weeks: the first sunny day in the calendar.
In a month: the big talk using the questions above and three agreements written down.

faq.q: Are we right for each other?
a: Lisovskaya’s method gives no compatibility percentages, so the honest answer is this: by the standards of her book your characters are well compatible, and your difficulties are clear and workable.

She checks the compatibility of characters by duals and half-duals. You both have the Fool as your dual, and for each it stands in the same point in the other’s matrix. What one wants in a relationship is the other’s spiritual purpose, crosswise. Far from every couple has such coincidences, and Lisovskaya herself stresses that even without them a union can rest on other, often deeper reasons.

What comes hard to you is visible too: in difficulties each withdraws, and in semi-darkness it is easy to imagine too much. This is a task, not a verdict. A couple with your matrix can live it as a constant chill, or as a rare ability to be close without getting in each other’s way and without losing each other. Which of these you get is up to you — and you decide it every day with small actions.

If you need a very short answer: you are right for each other as two people who feel good side by side in silence and who keep their word. For it to stay that way for years, you will have to learn one thing — to say out loud what each is used to understanding silently. This doesn’t change your characters: it is a skill, and you already have the support for it — Justice appears five times in the couple’s matrix.

faq.q: What does the Moon in the centre mean for us and what do we do with it?
a: The Moon in the centre means there is much understanding without words between you and much left unsaid. It is one trait with two sides. You sense each other more finely than most couples, and so you more easily make mistakes by taking your guess for knowledge.

Why sensing is not enough for you in particular is explained by your numbers: your two nines add up to 18, and this Moon stands in the very centre of the couple. One person’s silence turns into the other’s version by itself. So the Moon is worth translating into agreement in the most ordinary places — where it seems that “it’s obvious anyway”:

ul: You think your partner didn’t like a gift. Ask: “do you really like it or are you being polite?” — for Justice in your couple an honest answer is worth more than a polite one.
You decided they don’t want to visit your parents and declined for both in advance. Ask first.
In intimacy you want something different but feel the partner should understand anyway. Say it — Justice in your material point is responsible for this too.
It seemed to you that your purchase upset them. “Did this spending bother you?” settles the question in a minute; otherwise it will surface at the money evening.
You sense the partner wants change but isn’t saying so. Name it yourself: “it seems to me you feel cramped in our current routine — is that so?”

a: The Moon remains your gift as long as guesses reach a conversation and an agreement. Without that it becomes a source of hurt nobody wanted.

faq.q: We both love silence. Is that bad?
a: No. Silence is your shared values and common language; it joins you. It becomes bad when silence stops being rest and becomes a way of not talking about what is difficult.

It is easy to tell them apart. Good silence is named, it has an end, and after it you feel good together. Bad silence lasts several evenings, nobody talks about it, and after it things are colder between you. If the second kind has become frequent, start with the chapter on the couple’s tasks.

And remember the difference from the chapter on what fills you: silence restores each of you, while the couple is charged by light — shared impressions and joys. You will always have enough silence, but sunny days will have to be planned.

One more hint: look not at the amount of silence but at who chooses it. If both want a quiet evening, it is rest. If one wants to talk and the other has shut down, it is already a reason for a signal and a promise to come back to the talk tomorrow.

faq.q: What if we didn’t recognise ourselves?
a: It happens, and there are several reasons. The matrix shows strengths and forks in the road, not how you have already lived them. Perhaps you have long known how to talk about feelings, and the Moon’s minuses are unfamiliar to you. Then read the pluses — they are what you have already achieved.
The opposite happens too: a chapter seems foreign because its theme hasn’t arrived yet. Abundance through change, for example, opens up for many couples only after their first big shared decision.
Try doing the self-check separately and comparing the answers. Often one recognises the couple in what the other doesn’t, and that is a good reason to talk.

And another thing: the report describes the couple, not each of you separately. A person may not recognise themselves in the description of the couple because with other people they behave differently. The couple’s matrix shows exactly what arises between the two of you — so check whether you recognise your shared evenings, quarrels and decisions.

You can, and the matrix has a hint on how. Each of you earns through Justice — the middle of the money line is the same for both — so a venture where everything is written down suits you: shares, roles, deadlines. The Chariot in the couple’s second material point asks that each area has one person responsible.

By your personal points the roles fall into place by themselves. The February one, with Justice among their talents, is closer to contracts, accounting and quality. The September one, with the Emperor at the entrance to money, to the plan, structure and prices. The Star at the couple’s entrance to money suggests that what you should sell is what you do with inspiration.

The risk is the Hermit in the couple’s task. Work talks can crowd out talks about the two of you, and “not ready yet” can stretch for years. Give the shared venture deadlines, and give your life an evening a week when work isn’t discussed.

faq.q: What do the numbers 13 and 20 on the chart mean, which the report says almost nothing about?
a: The couple’s chart shows more numbers than the method reads. Lisovskaya doesn’t analyse every point in a couple, and here is what happens with the rest.

ul: **13 in the small point at the top and 11 in the inner circle above the centre** are an addition to the meeting point. According to the book they have no separate meaning: the main thing on this line is the meeting point itself, Strength.

**20 above the centre and 8 to the left of the centre** are two small points by the centre. Lisovskaya writes directly that they have nothing to do with the compatibility matrix: they are points for the health map and the chakras, which a couple doesn’t have.
**7 on the right ray** is an addition to the material point, the Chariot; it is covered in the chapter on money.

a: If you want to read the thirteen at least as a background: Death between two Strengths on the line of talents resembles a hint that your shared strength grows through ending old forms. This is our light interpretation, not a statement from the book. Interestingly, the same Death stands at the February one’s entrance to money.

faq.q: Our numbers in the lower right corner match. Does that mean we are the same?
a: In money and reconciliation — almost yes. The middle of the money line, the middle of the relationship line and the point where they cross are the same for you: 8, 4 and 22. You both earn by honest work under an agreement, order calms you both, you both need freedom.

But in the main thing you are different, and this can be seen in the chapter on what each brings to the couple. The centres are the Hanged Man and the Lovers: one likes to wait, the other to choose. The masks are the Hierophant and the World. The main talents are the Hermit and the High Priestess. The couple is made not of two identical people but of two different ones who are built the same way where money and reconciliation are decided. That is why agreeing about money is easy for you, while understanding each other in feelings takes work.

faq.q: Justice in the point “what joins you” — do we need to make our relationship official?
a: The matrix doesn’t say what to do with your status — that is for you alone to decide. It says you are joined by an honest word and clear agreements. Among the traits of Justice in a couple the book also names the wish to make the relationship official.

If the question is open for you and it worries one of you, it is better to discuss it directly and calmly than to wait for the other to guess. For a couple with the Moon in the centre, leaving such an important question unsaid is especially heavy. If you are both happy with things as they are, that is also an honest agreement, and it is enough to say it out loud.

If the talk about status has long been put off, recall the rule from the chapter on what each brings to the couple: the one who wants to wait names the waiting period. For such a question this is especially fair to both.

faq.q: We have lived together for a long time and everyday life has become routine. Where do we start?
a: With a sunny day. Routine for your couple is when only Justice and silence remain: chores are divided, promises kept, evenings calm. Everything is right, but there is little light. You are filled by the Sun: new impressions, celebrations, pride in each other.

For the coming month, choose one day together in a new place and one small shared event each week: breakfast out, a walk around an unfamiliar neighbourhood, an evening when each tells what they are proud of. And review the division of housework: sometimes routine rests on one unnoticed imbalance that one of you has kept quiet about for a year.

The third step is to bring back home a little of the Lovers, which the couple doesn’t have but each of you does: a passing touch, a compliment out loud, a shared decision about a small thing. Routine retreats when signs of attention appear again in an ordinary day.

One more hint is the Tower in the point of abundance. Sometimes routine is best broken not by a celebration but by a small change: rearrange the furniture, change your weekend routine, start something new together. For your couple a change chosen together means both money and freshness in the relationship.

faq.q: Why are there no chakras or age scale in the report?
a: Because a couple’s matrix doesn’t have them. Lisovskaya doesn’t look at chakras and ancestral lines in the compatibility matrix: these are tools of the personal matrix. She allows age periods to be read in a couple only as possible crisis periods and optionally — we don’t cover them in this report. A couple is read by its own points: image, atmosphere, meeting point, tasks, money, relationships, parenthood and values. If you want each of you analysed by chakras and ages, that is what a personal reading does.
